title: Is a guaranteed income enough if AI takes our jobs?
summary: Work gives people more than a pay cheque. In What is work for? Human wellbeing and the value of work in the AGI era, Chan, Jacobs and Cross draw on three new research papers to ask what that means if AI displaces human labour. A survey of more than 8,000 adults in the UK, US, Denmark and India finds that most people value their jobs for purpose, community and status as well as pay; in the UK, US and Denmark, about one in five would not leave their job even for a guaranteed income of up to 120% of their salary. Income support may be necessary in an AI transition, the authors conclude, but on its own it cannot replace the purpose, belonging and dignity that work provides.

title: Could AI concentrate power on an unprecedented scale?
summary: The gravest risk of advanced AI may come not from machines escaping human control, but from the people who control the machines. In The Political-Economic Risks of AI, Professor Carvalho sets out a scenario in which AI concentrates the global economy in a handful of firms, erodes democratic and egalitarian institutions, and causes human productivity to collapse. The closest precedent, he argues, is not earlier waves of automation but the devastation of indigenous societies under colonialism. To avert it, he proposes competition policy aimed at limiting the accumulation of economic control, stronger democratic institutions, including sortition, and sovereign AI for nations that can build it. You can also watch him discuss the political-economic risks of AI. Carvalho, Professor of Political Economy in Oxford’s Department of Economics, joins the Centre as a Faculty Affiliate.

title: Could physical AI create better manufacturing jobs?
summary: In a follow-up to his post on adaptive manufacturing, Professor Sentance asks what physical AI could mean for the people who work in factories. Manufacturers face around 500,000 unfilled openings for jobs few people want. Rather than shrinking the workforce, he argues, technologies that make production more accessible — from 3D printing to intelligent machines — could do for manufacturing what cheap film and digital video did for filmmaking: expand demand and create more attractive jobs.

title: Does worker retraining protect against automation?
summary: As AI raises fresh concerns about job displacement, retraining is often proposed as the answer. In Did US Worker Retraining Reduce Participant Automation Exposure?, Jacobs and Canedy test that idea using over 23 million records from the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, the main public funder of retraining in the United States. They find that participants rarely move into jobs less exposed to automation, and most return to their previous field. Where outcomes improve, it is mainly because wages recover, not because people change occupation. Employer-led apprenticeships do best.

title: Economic policy for AGI
summary: In one of the inaugural essays of the newly launched DeepMind Institute — a platform started by researchers at Google and Google DeepMind to publish and debate ideas about a world with AGI — Jacobs and Imas assess eleven policies for managing the economic disruption AGI could bring. Rather than a single prescription, they propose “least-regret” responses tied to clear empirical triggers: expanded unemployment insurance, tax credits, and employer-led retraining for mild disruption; a negative income tax if displacement deepens; and universal basic capital as a backstop should labour and capital income decouple.

title: What can physical AI actually do on the factory floor?
summary: After visiting a new deployment and IMTS in Chicago — the largest manufacturing technology show in North America — Professor Sentance asks what physical AI can really do in a factory. A century of process engineering has been about removing variation, he argues, so AI’s great strength — adapting to the unfamiliar — adds little to today’s linear production lines. The real opportunity lies in the adaptive, non-linear processes that manufacturers abandoned because they were too unpredictable to manage or too dangerous for people.

title: Finding causal relationships in incomplete data
summary: In “PAIR-CI: Calibrated Conditional Independence Testing for Causal Discovery with Incomplete Data”, Robinson and Lall introduce a machine learning method for uncovering causal relationships in data with missing values — a pervasive problem in the surveys, firm records, and cross-national datasets that social scientists rely on. Where existing approaches can mistake gaps in the data for genuine causal links, the new method keeps such false discoveries rare. The paper will appear at NeurIPS 2026, the premier venue for research in artificial intelligence and machine learning.

title: The chain of peace: do supply chain chokepoints deter war?
summary: Advanced semiconductors cannot be made by any one country. Design software is American, lithography machines Dutch, optics German, photoresists Japanese, fabrication Taiwanese — and remove any node and the chain breaks. Pham and Scholten argue that this structure, not Taiwan's foundries alone, is what deters conflict in the Taiwan Strait, because a chip fab seized by force produces nothing without the network behind it. The uncomfortable implication is that export controls and reshoring, each sensible in isolation, are steadily dismantling the interdependence that keeps the peace.
